title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district perceived generative AI, especially chatbot tools such as ChatGPT, shortly after these tools became widely available. The authors ask whether teachers’ reactions differ by grade band taught, subject area, and years of teaching experience, and what concerns, perceived benefits, and professional development (PD) needs teachers report for themselves and for students.

The study is not an intervention trial; instead, it uses districtwide survey data supplemented by qualitative coding of open-ended responses. The survey was administered to certificated educators in a large West Coast urban district in 2023, producing 1,454 complete teacher responses. Teachers reported their AI chatbot usage, allowability policies for student use, concerns, benefits, and PD needs. Quantitative analyses used logistic regression and chi-square tests, while qualitative responses were coded thematically.

The sample included elementary, middle, and high school teachers, with comparisons also made by subject area for middle/high school teachers (STEM, humanities, and other) and by experience level (less than vs. more than 10 years). The findings show that willingness to allow AI use decreased as grade level increased, and more experienced teachers were generally more restrictive. Elementary and middle school teachers most often wanted basic AI literacy, while high school teachers more often wanted guidance on how to manage student AI use and detect AI-generated work.

Overall, the paper concludes that teacher attitudes toward generative AI are strongly shaped by instructional context and experience, suggesting that AI-related PD and policy should be differentiated by grade band and teaching role. It also highlights that teachers distinguish sharply between AI’s possible uses for teachers versus students, with different perceived benefits and risks for each.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI chatbot / large language model system used for conversational text generation, answering questions, and assisting with tasks such as writing support, concept explanation, code generation, and lesson-planning help.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed K-12 teachers’ perceptions, allowability, concerns, and professional development needs related to generative AI chatbots in schools; the paper explicitly references ChatGPT as an example but does not study a specific product beyond generic chatbot use.

findings.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of 1,454 teachers in a large urban school district, teachers in secondary settings were less willing to allow generative AI chatbot use than elementary teachers. More experienced elementary teachers (>10 years) were also significantly less likely to allow AI for idea generation, paper editing, writing entire papers, concept explanation, and code generation; the paper reports marginal effects such as dy/dx = -0.489 for idea generation and -0.500 for code generation in elementary settings.
findings.measure: Teachers’ allowability / willingness to permit student use of AI chatbots for idea generation, editing/completing a paper, writing a paper, explaining a concept, and generating code
findings.effect_size: dy/dx = -0.121 to -0.150 by grade level; elementary more-experienced teacher dy/dx = -0.489 to -0.587 across writing-support outcomes
findings.confidence_interval: see paper tables; e.g., grade-level models 95% CI [ -0.126, -0.116 ] to [ -0.156, -0.144 ]; elementary more-experienced models 95% CI [ -0.633, -0.346 ] to [ -0.826, -0.348 ]

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ reported professional development needs varied significantly by grade level (χ²_dof=21 = 63.949, p=0.000), but not by subject or experience level. Elementary and middle school teachers emphasized basic AI literacy, while high school teachers emphasized how to instruct/manage student AI use and how to detect AI-generated work.
findings.measure: Open-ended professional development needs coded by grade level, subject, and years of experience
findings.sample_size: n=1,454; coded needs analyses reported for subgroups

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods cross-sectional survey study, not an experiment. It provides subgroup analyses and coded qualitative responses, but causal inference is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported subgroup differences are meaningful for implementation and professional development, but the study does not test an intervention and the effect sizes are mostly directional/marginal rather than outcome impacts on learning.
